newsitem.title: UK: British police charge man in IRA Docklands bombing.
newsitem.headline: British police charge man in IRA Docklands bombing.

text.p: British police on Friday charged a man in connection with a deadly bomb attack in London's Docklands residential and office district that ended the IRA's ceasefire in February 1996.
The bomb in the Docklands business district killed two people and marked the end of a 17-month ceasefire by Irish Republican Army guerrillas fighting to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Police said the man charged with the incident would appear at a London court on Saturday afternoon on two counts of murder and conspiracy to cause an explosion.
"He has been charged with an IRA explosion. We are releasing no details prior to the court appearance," a police spokesman said.
Security sources in Northern Ireland said the man was among seven people arrested on Saturday in a raid on a farmhouse near Crosmaglen in Northern Ireland.
He was flown to London early on Thursday, they said.

News of the charge came hours after a series of suspected IRA bomb warnings paralysed rail and road traffic in northern England in what appeared to be the latest attempt by the guerrillas to disrupt Britain's election campaign.
There were small explosions at railway stations in Doncaster and Leeds in northern England.
In Leeds, a large part of the city centre was sealed off after the explosion for which there was no warning.
Stoke, Doncaster and Crewe railway station were all closed after police were told of telephoned bomb warnings in which the caller gave a codeword known to be used by the outlawed IRA.
A large section of the main M6 motorway, linking southern Britain with the northwest, was also closed after a phone call threatening a bomb explosion.
The M6 closure was near a sports stadium that Prime Minister John Major was due to visit on Friday.

Major pinned the incidents on the IRA, which has admitted causing similar incidents earlier in the campaign for a May 1 election and has often employed tactics that cause maximum chaos, thereby winning maximum attention, but no loss of life.
"This looks very much at the moment as though this is the work of the IRA showing their usual contempt for people's lives and for property," Major said.
